# 4 Benchmarks (continued)

## THE ROLE OF BENCHMARKS {#a}

Benchmarks are crucial for the relationship between asset owners and asset managers. Even prior to considering this relationship, benchmarks will be needed to model liabilities, establish diversification opportunities and determine asset allocations. Asset owners will carefully select benchmarks to articulate objectives, communicate risk tolerances and ultimately evaluate performance. Typically, benchmark relationships can be described as:

**(1) *Passive***

The investment strategy is to replicate the benchmark precisely or as closely as possible. In effect the investment decision process has been delegated to the index provider.

**(2) *Relative***

Investment decisions are made explicitly in relation to benchmark weights, exposures and risk. Most active management relationships will fall into this category.

**(3) *Aware***

Investment decisions are not directly tied to benchmark weights or risk, but the benchmark description articulates the broad strategy and universe from which securities may be chosen.

**(4) *Agnostic***

In this relationship the benchmark is background information, a market barometer potentially, often a target return, and perhaps used in reporting as a reference to provide some context and certainly not closely referenced by the asset manager.

## TYPES OF BENCHMARKS {#b}

There are many types of benchmarks used in the evaluation of portfolio performance:

1. Commercial indexes
2. Customised indexes
3. Peer groups
4. Random portfolios
5. Exchange-traded funds (ETFs)
6. Target (or absolute) returns
7. Blended benchmarks
8. Spliced benchmarks
9. Money-weighted benchmarks (or public market equivalents)
10. Normal portfolio
